item.title: Better Models: Worse Tools
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Armin Ronacher spent two days chasing a strange bug and came away with a broader worry about where model training is heading. His writeup starts from a concrete regression: the newest Claude models call a third-party editor tool with invented, schema-breaking fields, and they do it more than their predecessors did.

The uncomfortable lesson is that tool schemas are not neutral, at least not on Anthropic models. We like to pretend that a schema is an abstract contract and the model is a general reasoner that will follow it, but that might no longer be the case for some of the tools.

The bug

  • The failing call. Ronacher traced a Pi issue in which newer Claude models call Pi’s file-edit tool with extra, invented fields inside its nested edits[] array. Not a small model: Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 5 too. The edit content is usually correct, but the arguments break the schema, so Pi rejects the call and the model has to retry.
  • Worse in the newer models. Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 both show it, and none of the older models in the family do. Across trials the invented keys were a whole zoo: type, id, requireUnique, matchCase, in_file, oldText2, newText2, even an event.0.additionalProperties. The oldText and newText payloads themselves came out byte-correct, and the model only appended nonsense at the end of the object.
  • Only under agentic history. A fresh, single-turn “edit this file” prompt never reproduced it. An agentic history, where the model had read files, diagnosed a problem, and composed a multi-line edit, did. In one user’s transcripts, continuing the session made Opus 4.8 fail about 20% of the time. Stripping the thinking blocks from the history halved the rate, and turning on strict tool invocation eliminated it.

How tool calls actually work

  • Tool calls are just text. The client folds the transcript, system prompt, and tool list into one large prompt with special marker tokens, and the model, trained on that format, emits something the client reads back as “call this tool with these arguments.” Anthropic’s format, glimpsed from leaked markers, looks XML-ish, with <invoke> and <parameter> tags. A top-level string parameter appears inline, but an array of objects is serialized as JSON inside the parameter.
  • Two routes to a valid structure. One is to ask the model for schema-conforming JSON and validate it afterward. The other is to constrain the sampler so invalid tokens cannot be emitted at all, which is grammar-aware (or constrained) decoding: if the schema allows only oldText and newText, the sampler can stop the model from ever emitting in_file. Without constraints, the model is only following a learned convention.

Why it’s getting worse

  • A training-time cause. Ronacher’s hypothesis is that the regression comes from how the newest models were post-trained rather than from random deterioration. Older Claude models were trained before a shipped harness like Claude Code was the obvious target. Newer ones are post-trained inside Claude Code, or a close simulation of it, so they learn what a successful call looks like there and which mistakes that environment tolerates.
  • A forgiving client. Claude Code’s own edit tool is flat: file_path, old_string, new_string, and an optional replace_all, nothing like Pi’s nested edits[]. Claude Code ships closed-source, as a minified JavaScript bundle, but reading that bundle Ronacher finds parameter aliases (old_str alongside old_string, path for file_path), type coercions, Unicode repair, and silent filtering of unknown keys. It does not use strict mode, because Anthropic’s complexity limits on strict tool definitions would make those API calls fail.
  • No gradient against slop. When reinforcement learning runs inside a harness that forgiving, a slightly malformed call still completes the task and still earns reward. Little gradient pushes back against inventing an alias or adding a stray field. Worse, the model builds a strong prior for Claude Code’s exact shape, so a tool with the same intent but a different schema is increasingly off-distribution, and a better-trained model resists it more rather than less. Ronacher notes that Opus 4.5 adapted to foreign edit tools unusually well, and worries the trend has since reversed.

What it means for harnesses

  • Where the bad keys appear. They are not random. They cluster at the highest-entropy point of the task, right after the model closes a several-hundred-token escaped newText string and must choose between } and , "...". Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 appear to have learned that an edit may take one extra optional field, but under Pi’s nested shape they have no trained name for it, so they sample a plausible name fresh each time. That is why the failures produce dozens of different keys rather than one stable alias.
  • OpenAI documents its format. OpenAI’s open-weight gpt-oss models are trained on a documented response format, harmony, which puts an in-band <|constrain|>json marker in the transcript so the inference stack knows exactly when to switch into JSON-constrained sampling. Anthropic’s models and harness are both closed. Strict mode does fix the bug, which suggests the server refuses to sample a key the schema does not permit, and that in turn explains why strict tool definitions come with a complexity cap.
  • Schemas are not neutral. A model can understand a schema and still be bad at emitting it under pressure, because some shapes sit close to what post-training rewarded and some sit far away. Ronacher, once skeptical of constrained decoding for its quality tradeoffs, says this bug moved his priors. And the more post-training concentrates inside one dominant, undocumented harness, the more every other harness inherits its quirks.

My Notes

  • The benchmark blind spot. If Ronacher’s hypothesis is right, a model like Opus 4.8 could score higher on coding benchmarks and still be worse at this particular call, because those benchmarks run inside forgiving harnesses that repair the exact slop Pi rejects. On that reading, a benchmark score reflects the model together with the harness it runs in, so a higher number need not mean higher reliability against an arbitrary tool schema. The open-weights gap analysis made the same point in a different setting: a forgiving shared harness can make a weaker model look stronger than it is, narrowing the apparent distance to the closed frontier.

  • Harness choice is now partly fixed at training time. Harness Engineering treats the harness as a runtime layer chosen around a fixed model. This regression suggests the reverse: some of the harness is set during training, so a team that adopts a different harness inherits the training harness’s schema habits whether or not they fit its own tools.

  • Who absorbs the mismatch. Tuning models to Claude Code’s tool shapes imposes a cost on every third-party agent that uses a different schema, in retries and rejected calls, and the one fix, strict constrained decoding, is off by default with a complexity cap that rejects nested schemas like Pi’s. Because the client and Anthropic’s training setup are both closed, those teams also cannot see why, inferring the cause from the minified bundle and from behavior, as Ronacher did. Whether Anthropic intends it or not, that is a mild form of lock-in.

Related Posts

  • Harness Engineering: the case that the harness around a model accounts for much of an agent’s reliability, which this post turns into a warning: the harness a model was trained in also shapes what it can reliably emit.
  • Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems: a map of Claude Code as a harness, the dominant one whose flat edit schema Ronacher says the model now over-fits to.
  • Claude Opus 4.8: The Early Reactions: the model at the center of this regression, seen from the other side of the capability story.
  • How Far Behind the Closed Frontier Are Open-Weights LLMs?: makes the same model-plus-harness point in a different setting, where a shared forgiving harness can narrow the apparent gap between open and closed models.
  • How Claude Code Works in Large Codebases: Best Practices and Where to Start: practical use of the exact tools whose canonical shape, Ronacher argues, has become a prior the model defends.

item.title: SpudCell: A Synthetic Cell Built From Scratch That Divides
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Scientists have built something that behaves like a living cell: it takes in food, grows, splits in two, and even evolves a little over a few generations, all without starting from any living thing. Every part was purified in a lab and put together from scratch. It isn’t alive, and it stops working after a handful of divisions, but it gives researchers a fully known, built-from-parts system for studying how the first cells might have come together.

Kate Adamala’s lab at the University of Minnesota has built SpudCell, a cell-like system assembled entirely from purified, non-living components that runs a full cell cycle. I read it through two sources: Biotic’s own announcement page and Ars Technica’s write-up, which frame the same result very differently.

What the work reports:

  • SpudCell is built bottom-up from a defined parts list: a ~90,000-base-pair genome across seven DNA plasmids, the PURE protein-expression system (36 purified E. coli enzymes, including ribosomes), and a lipid membrane. Earlier minimal-cell work — the JCVI-syn3.0 cell (Hutchison et al., 2016) — carved a living cell down to 473 genes. This one assembles from individually purified pieces.
  • It feeds by fusing with “feeder liposomes” that deliver lipids and nutrients. A protein SpudCell makes from its own DNA (α-hemolysin, tagged) locks onto the feeder membrane and triggers fusion, so the genome controls whether and how fast the cell grows.
  • It divides without a cytoskeleton: the surface protein crowds until mechanical stress makes the membrane bud off. Cells that make more of it divide more efficiently.
  • Selection works. A genetic change raising fusion-protein output let those cells outgrow the original over five generations, more so under nutrient scarcity.
  • The limits are steep. Plasmids distribute randomly at division, so after five generations only ~30% of daughters carry all seven. The cell also can’t remake its borrowed E. coli ribosomes, so it runs 5–10 generations before the machinery degrades. The manuscript is a preprint, not yet peer-reviewed.

My Notes

  • Have we created life? No. SpudCell borrows its ribosomes from E. coli and can’t make new ones, and it can’t pass its genome to daughter cells reliably. It runs on machinery that real organisms evolved over billions of years, and it winds down once the borrowed pieces wear out. Making life would mean building a system that produces and inherits its own machinery. SpudCell is useful because it doesn’t do that yet: it lets researchers test which of the missing pieces matter most, and in what order they would have had to appear.

  • Two sources, two framings: Biotic’s page leads with “the first synthetic cell with a complete cell cycle” and a genome smaller than the 113 kbp that prior analysis had speculated as the minimum for a living cell, while Ars Technica leads with “it only works for a few divisions thanks to a lot of added materials.” Both are accurate, though “complete cell cycle” is generous: the system divides but does not reliably inherit, since each daughter gets a random draw of plasmids and nothing ran past five generations. The announcement sells the milestone and the write-up stresses how much external machinery it needs, and the honest read of the result holds the two together.

  • Selection worked, but only briefly: getting real Darwinian selection to run on chemistry built from a parts list is the genuine result. The demonstration was small and heavily engineered, and the advantage held only for the few generations before genome loss shut everything down. Whether selection can do more depends on first fixing how the genome is passed on.

Related Posts

  • Reverse Engineering the BioNTech/Pfizer Vaccine: the same view of biology as legible, engineerable code, read off a molecule rather than built into one.
  • The Neuroscience of Consciousness: Peter Tse on The Gradient: the mind-side companion to the same bottom-up move, asking what minimal physical system is enough to count.

item.title: What It Means to Be a Mathematician When AI Does the Math
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

IEEE Spectrum surveys how working mathematicians are reacting as AI systems start to conjecture, prove, and formalize, and finds the community split over what its own role should become.

What the article reports:

  • Recent milestones: gold-medal performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad by Google DeepMind and OpenAI systems, DeepMind’s Aletheia autonomously producing a publishable PhD-level result in arithmetic geometry, an OpenAI model disproving a combinatorial-geometry conjecture, and Math, Inc.’s Gauss formalizing the 24-dimensional case of Maryna Viazovska’s sphere-packing proof in two weeks.

  • Three camps are emerging: AI as a tool (human understanding matters most), AI as a partner (shared discovery), and AI as an oracle (only the answers matter).

  • The researchers the piece interviews divide along that split:

    • Yang-Hui He (London Institute for Mathematical Sciences) voices the oracle worry: if machines hand down answers no one grasps, human mathematicians could become “priests to oracles.”
    • Akshay Venkatesh (Princeton, Fields Medalist) takes the human-centric view he first pressed at his 2022 Fields Medal Symposium, asking not just what computers can do but what mathematics is for — for him numbers are “a way of bringing us to agreement,” and he worries the years-long struggle to understand a proof may become hard to justify to funders and to mathematicians themselves.
    • Maia Fraser (University of Ottawa) shares that stance: even when a machine settles a question, coming up with “an elegant, beautiful human proof” remains “a valuable endeavor,” because the struggle to understand is one of the discipline’s greatest rewards.
    • Terence Tao (UCLA, Fields Medalist) is the collaborative voice: his “big mathematics” is large decentralized human-AI projects where formalization in proof assistants like Lean establishes trust through verification rather than reputation, so an idea from an unknown or an amateur counts if the formal proof checks.

  • The risks the piece names: accessibility (math becoming compute-gated and elitist), motivation (why spend years understanding what a machine can produce?), and intellectual atrophy in students who skip the struggle.

My Notes

  • Understanding is the step AI leaves behind: Tao has split doing mathematics into generation, verification, and digestion — producing a proof, checking it, and actually understanding it. AI is fast at the first two and slow at the third. The article’s motivation worry is that last gap: if a machine can hand you a checked proof, the years of effort spent understanding it start to look optional, felt as a loss of purpose rather than a missing capability.

  • The elitism risk cuts against an open-weight counter-trend: the article’s worry is that compute-gated frontier models make math pay-to-play, inverting a discipline that needed only pen, paper, and training. That holds only if the useful systems stay proprietary. Open-weight models have stayed close behind the frontier, so whether math becomes elitist depends on how wide the proprietary gap grows. The risk is real but conditional.

  • Verification covers only the proof step: formalization catches errors at the proof step, which is why Tao says it “filters out a lot of the rubbish.” But the trust chain still includes whether the formal statement faithfully captures the informal one, and whether the checker itself is sound. A Claude agent once found a buffer overflow in the Lean runtime under formally verified code, so even “checked in Lean” leaves the formalization and the checker outside the guarantee.

Related Posts

  • Proof Generation vs Digestion: Tao’s own generation/verification/digestion decomposition, the frame underneath the article’s motivation worry.
  • The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics: the community-guardrails response that the article’s closing turn to workshops and guidelines points toward.
  • Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search: a concrete instance of Tao’s formalization-as-trust vision, closing open Erdős and OEIS problems in Lean.
  • An OpenAI Model Disproves a Discrete-Geometry Conjecture: the combinatorial-geometry milestone the article cites, with external mathematicians doing the checking.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the thesis that formal math is the deterministic pillar under a probabilistic LLM stack, the industrial version of Tao’s trust argument.

item.title: AI Detectors Are Reliable Enough to Be Dangerous
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The Atlantic profiles Pangram, the AI-writing detector behind most recent high-profile accusations, and argues that a detector accurate enough to trust but not accurate enough to be right is the more dangerous kind.

What the article reports:

  • Pangram has become the de facto standard. It was behind a horror novel pulled days before release, accusations against articles in The New York Times, prize-winning short stories, and parts of Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical, and it is used by universities and scientific associations. It connects to Canvas, so teachers can scan student submissions at scale.
  • Pangram claims a false-positive rate near one in 10,000, and a University of Chicago analysis found almost no false positives on ~3,000 sample texts. But its false-negative rate is closer to one in 70, and “humanizer” tools like Walter Writes AI reliably flipped AI text to “human-written” in the author’s tests.
  • CEO Max Spero says Pangram should “never be the ending arbiter” but a starting point, and concedes the model’s inner workings are “pretty uninterpretable.” Its “AI-assisted” label spans everything from a grammar check to near-ghostwriting.
  • Real accusations are already misfiring: a Wall Street Journal editor called Pangram a “defamation machine,” and Pangram itself later found it had wrongly flagged a Taylor Lorenz story. The piece compares the coming AI-detection wars to the 2023–24 plagiarism-detection accusations.

My Notes

  • The base-rate problem: with more than 30 million US students each turning in dozens of assignments, even a one-in-10,000 false-positive rate produces a steady stream of wrongful accusations. The problem is structural, and it is the one that survives every improvement to the model.

  • The “AI-assisted” label: collapsing grammar-check, thesaurus use, brainstorming, and near-ghostwriting into a single category means the detector cannot draw the line that actually matters, and neither can the person acting on its verdict. That is an ontology problem no amount of calibration fixes.

  • Non-stationary accuracy: the labs optimize for human-sounding output and humanizer tools exist specifically to defeat detectors, which makes detecting AI text an adversarial moving target. Any third-party audit is months old on arrival, so an institution citing a 95% accuracy figure is quoting a number that no longer describes the tool. This is the same theme as celebrating human work rather than trying to certify its absence of AI.

  • The black-box accusation: Pangram cannot say why it flagged a passage, so an appeal has nothing to contest. That is the same divide as catching a lying LLM with a black-box test versus one that can point inside the model, and it is why the plagiarism-detection comparison in the article is apt: those tools were also opaque, also trusted, and also wrong often enough to ruin people.

Related Posts

  • Not AI Generated: the inverse response, certifying and celebrating human work instead of trying to detect the absence of AI.
  • arXiv: Unchecked LLM-Generated Content Can Trigger a One-Year Submission Ban: an institution acting on AI-content evidence, with the same enforcement stakes.
  • Influential ChatGPT-in-Education Meta-Analysis Retracted: the education-stakes context and the cost of trusting an unaccountable result.
  • AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance: the underlying reason students reach for AI that detection then tries to police.

item.title: The Easy Interval Method: Intervals Every Day, Run Easy
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In this 13-minute explainer, Terry O’Hare, a masters runner from Ireland who runs the Faster Master channel, lays out the Easy Interval Method (EIM), a training system devised by Dutch coach Herman Verheul in the 1970s and developed by Dutch 5,000 m runner Klaas Lok [1]. The pitch is counterintuitive: instead of building a base from long, slow endurance runs, you run intervals almost every day, but at a sub-threshold pace, with recoveries long enough that you can back it up the next day.

The main points, each linking to the supporting part of the transcript:

  • The workload is survivable because of pace and recovery. Intervals run six days a week are possible because they sit at sub-threshold pace with a recovery jog roughly equal to the rep, plus a short walk at each end, so you can complete the session today and repeat it tomorrow.
  • The long recovery is the point. Far from being a concession, an 800–1,000 m jog recovery covers real aerobic mileage a static 90-second rest never would, which is why critics who want to shorten it miss what the system is doing.
  • Even skeptics can steal the surges. If daily intervals aren’t for you, adding short pickups (surges) to an ordinary long run captures much of the benefit and turns the run into an impromptu fartlek.

My Notes

  • Where the easy mileage goes. EIM accumulates aerobic stimulus without the neuromuscular cost of hard intervals or the staleness of slow steady running. The recovery jog does the easy-volume work that steady-state runs do in a conventional plan, while the daily reps keep some pace and leg reactivity in the system. That is why “intervals every day” is less reckless than it first sounds, once you see where the easy mileage goes.
  • Versus Norwegian singles. The contrast Terry draws with the Norwegian singles method is the useful reference point for anyone who has met that trend. Both hold reps at sub-threshold, and the only real difference is scheduling. Norwegian singles pack the sub-threshold work into a few days and fill the rest with easy running. EIM spreads it across almost every day and lets the long recovery jog absorb the easy running.
  • The evidence caveat. What the video lacks is evidence. The case rests on one athlete’s palmares, one masters record-holder, and a coach’s rationale, with no controlled comparison against a matched training plan. That is normal for training-methodology content, but a reader deciding whether to switch should treat the mechanism story as plausible rather than proven, and ramp in gradually as Terry himself insists.

Transcript

What’s here is the video’s auto-generated transcript, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The spoken words are preserved; three layers of editorial structure have been added on top:

  • Topic outline. The video has no official YouTube chapters, so the [12] section headings below are my own segmentation of the talk. Each links to the video at the timestamp where that section begins.
  • Inline hyperlinks. First mention of a salient name, concept, or product links to an authoritative source.
  • Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag a claim worth confirming or a spot where the auto-captions garbled a figure.

This is a single-speaker video, so there are no per-paragraph speaker labels — the whole body is Terry O’Hare talking. Because the source is auto-captions, punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks are editorial (ASR ships without them), and obvious mishearings of names and terms are corrected silently — e.g. the captions’ Class Lactate, EAM, and EIAM are rendered as Klaas Lok, EIM, and the garbled PSS 4 200 m as paces for 200 m.

0:00 — The club-runner rut, and a Dutch alternative

A lot of runners, particularly club runners, training 5 or 6 days a week, can get into a bit of a cycle of long run Sunday, during the week maybe one, two speed sessions Tuesday and Thursday, and the rest of the week they just fill in with long, easy, or recovery runs. And of course, time has shown that this can work for many of us. But is there a better way?

Well, back in the 1970s, Dutch coach Herman Verheul, I think that’s how you pronounce it, turned traditional thinking on its head. Instead of slow, easy endurance runs as the basis of all training, he introduced a system consisting almost entirely of interval training. It was then popularized and continually developed by Dutch 5,000 m runner Klaas Lok, and it is now widely known as EIM, easy interval method. So, if your training has become a bit monotonous, or your race times have stagnated, perhaps it’s time to look at a different approach.

I’m Terry O’Hare, a masters runner from Ireland. This is the Faster Masters channel, and if you haven’t already done so, it would really help the channel if you give it a thumbs up like, and hit the subscribe button. Thank you.

1:24 — What the method actually is

So, let’s look at this in a bit more depth. It could be said, and has been said, that lots of long, slow endurance runs create long, slow endurance runners. But are intervals 6 days a week a real, viable alternative? Is it actually possible?

In the EIM, sustained easy or steady-state runs are virtually nonexistent. For all distances other than the marathon, and occasionally the half marathon, the traditional weekly long run disappears too. And even when included, in the marathon schedules, it will contain surges. More of that later.

2:05 — Why daily intervals are possible: easy pace and long recovery

So is it physically possible to run intervals every day, six days a week, without breaking down very quickly? Well, the clue is in the name, easy, and made possible by both the pace of the run and the length of the recovery period.

The intervals, normally 200 m, 400 m, and 1,000 m repeats, with the occasional 2,000, will have an equal or near-equal recovery. So 200s will have a 200 easy recovery, 400s will have a 400 recovery, and 1,000 m repeats will have 800, maybe even 1,000 m recovery. And furthermore, at the finish of each rep, you will actually walk 30 to 40 m, and walk again before the start of the next one.

Then there’s the speed of each interval. These are not run at the pace we would normally consider interval pace. Instead, these are very much sub-threshold pace — a bit of a buzzword at the moment with the Norwegian singles — but I’ll give you some idea of the actual pace times in a minute so you get the idea.

3:08 — A sample half-marathon week

Let’s look at a typical week’s training for a runner preparing for a half marathon and training six days a week. Sunday, and being a half marathon program, there is actually a moderate endurance run here, 14 to 18K, but with surges, which we’re going to look at later, and also three to five times 100 m strides. Monday, 10 by 400. Tuesday, six by 1,000. Wednesday, six by 1,000. Thursday, 15 by 200s. Friday, six by 1,000. And a rest day Saturday. And there’s a few strides thrown in there three or four days a week, whenever you can manage it. And the intervals Monday to Friday would of course have three or 4 k warm-up and the same cool-down.

Now, before you say that’s excessive, just remember these intervals are not run at your 3k or 5k race pace with a 60s and 90-second recovery. No, they’re run very much at a sub-threshold pace.

4:11 — How it differs from Norwegian singles

So, are these similar to Norwegian singles? Well, Norwegian singles are also run at a sub-threshold pace, maybe a little quicker, but the big difference is in the recovery. The recovery with the EIM is designed so that you can recover sufficiently, not only to finish the session, but to do it again tomorrow and the next day and the next day, five or six times a week. With Norwegian singles, you do them all on three separate days a week and just fill in the rest with easy recovery runs.

4:42 — Pace comparison: Daniels’ VDOT versus Lok’s charts

Maybe the easiest way to demonstrate the actual pace would be to compare interval times calculated, for example, by renowned coach Jack Daniels and his VDOT system with Klaas Lok’s EIM times. Let’s take a 40-minute 10k runner as an example. Using the well-known Jack Daniels VDOT charts, 1,000 intervals for a 40-minute 10k runner would be run at between 3:43 and 3:55 pace. With Klaas Lok’s EIM system, these would be run at 4:14 to 4:31 pace. A substantial difference.

And furthermore, Daniels would recommend a recovery time equal to about half of the time of the interval. So, in this example, about 2 minutes. Whereas with the easy interval method, you would have an 800-meter recovery plus a little walk at the start and finish, maybe looking at 6, 7 minutes. All of a sudden, it looks a bit — or a lot — easier. And there would be a similar percentage difference in the paces for 200 m and 400 m intervals.

5:45 — Easing in, and the claimed benefits

Nevertheless, even though this is beginning to sound a lot easier than at first sight, there is no way that someone doing four, five easy runs a week could switch to this immediately. You would definitely have to introduce it gradually. If you’re already doing, however, one or two faster workouts a week, consider changing those to 1,000 m repeats, and you would actually find that easier. Then you’d be in a position to consider adding a third day for a few weeks, maybe 400s.

So, the claimed advantages to using this system would be more reactivity in the legs from running at a faster than easy pace. That in turn would give a better running economy and improved biomechanics. The ability to run at a higher speed without excess lactate in the muscles. And you’d be fitter and better prepared for races. Is it suited for masters runners? I think it’s ideal for masters runners to maintain your speed and reactive running.

6:48 — Why the recoveries are so long

Why are the recovery periods so long? Critics will say that 800 m or 1,000 m jog recovery is far too long, and the intervals at that sub-threshold pace could be done with 60 to 90-second recovery. But this longer recovery is as crucial to the system as the pace. A full 800, 1,000 m jog provides far greater aerobic stimulus than a static 90-second rest, simply due to the actual mileage being covered.

And remember that, just as with normal intervals, where you don’t do the first few too hard and then struggle to complete the session, they need to be at this easy controlled pace not only to complete the session today, but to repeat it tomorrow and the next day and the next day. This is high-end aerobic training at its best, and this is the key.

7:51 — Surges: the one long run, done differently

I mentioned earlier that one long endurance run is included in the marathon training and sometimes in the half marathon schedule. But there’s a slight, or big, important difference to how this is run. Every endurance run includes surges. Now, surges are when you pick up the pace to maybe 10k race pace for 30 to 60 seconds every 5 to 7 minutes.

I’ve tried this. What I do is when my Garmin beeps at each kilometer, I pick up the pace for 200 m, back off again. Simple as that. And what a difference that makes to your run. Doing this on a long run over varied terrain almost turns this into a fartlek session, in that I have no idea before I start where the 1k markers are going to hit. They could be on a nice flat even surface, or they could be at the bottom of a steep hill. And that makes the run more fun.

I regularly do a 20k run like this. I use the first 2k of that as a warm-up and then add the 200 surges each kilometer, and I end up with a 20k run that has included 18 by 200s at about 10k pace without noticing any extra effort. It’s a very useful workout that is fun and it’s over before you realize it.

You can look at this system and decide all those intervals are not for me. At least take the surges out of this. Add them into your long run. They will transform your long run and you will enjoy it.

9:25 — No VO2 max work, and racing as the anaerobic stimulus

As I mentioned earlier, this is high-end aerobic training. There is no VO2 max workout here, and that could be an issue for some. Klaas himself raced very regularly and used a lot of those races as anaerobic workouts. And regular racing is almost assumed with this system. For those who don’t, including myself, there are anaerobic sessions included in the plans, and to be used particularly in the build-up to racing.

9:57 — Who it suits: Lok, masters reactivity, and Dan King

So, who is this type of training suited to? Well, Klaas Lok himself admits, or claims, that he was not naturally very talented or gifted, but he still used to win 26 Dutch national titles, including six cross-country championships, a 10,000 m title, a 1,500 m title, and a European indoor silver in the 3,000 m in 1980.

Note

Editor’s note. The auto-captions garble the specific personal-best times Terry lists here (the raw ASR reads “a 20 at 24 10,000 m, a 330 at 1,500 m”), so the mistranscribed numbers have been dropped rather than guessed at. See the book for Lok’s actual bests.

Now, some coaches believe that us masters runners shouldn’t be doing interval training at all because our muscle reactivity has declined with age, but EIM actually promotes the opposite. Reactivity is a basic essential which should be maintained at your highest possible personal level. Not only are strong reactive muscles faster, they’re also less prone to injury.

A masters runner you might have heard of who is an exponent of the EIM is Dan King, a US male 60 to 65 runner who, in one day in 2020, set a world mile record of 4:52, an American record of 9:58 in the 3,000 m, and a US 5,000 m record of 16:48. And yes, all in one day.

Note

Editor’s note. This checks out: on December 11, 2020, Dan King (then 61) ran 4:52 for the mile, 9:58.47 for the 3,000 m, and 16:48.67 for the 5,000 m in a single day, the latter two ratified as M60 American records (per Runner’s World and Bring Back the Mile). Age-group records move, so treat “world record” as of that date.

11:31 — The book and the community

To get a complete insight into this system, you really need to read this book, unsurprisingly titled The Easy Interval Method [1]. It really is a bible, and it’s a mine of information. I just flicked through a few pages and you’ll see how well worn it is with me. I refer to it almost on a daily basis. It contains everything: schedules from 800 m to marathon. It has pace charts, everything you would ever need as a runner. Have a look on Google for this, The Easy Interval Method by Klaas Lok. And it has schedules for runners who can only commit to 3 days a week right up to those who want to train 7, 8 times a week. Buy it, you will not regret it.

Buying the book will give you access to the Facebook group where ex-runners of the system and Klaas Lok himself will answer your questions, respond to your comments, which is incredibly useful as you progress through a training plan.

So, if you enjoyed this video, please hit the subscribe button, you know it makes sense. And if you want to find out more about the alternative Norwegian singles training, watch my most successful ever video here. And of course, don’t forget to look at our brand new website, thefastermaster.com. For now, though, thank you for watching.

People

  • Terry O’Hare / the Faster Master — masters runner from Ireland; the video’s presenter.
  • Klaas Lok — Dutch 5,000 m runner and coach who developed and popularized the Easy Interval Method.
  • Herman Verheul — Dutch coach who originated the interval-based approach in the 1970s that became the EIM.
  • Jack Daniels — running coach and physiologist; creator of the VDOT system referenced in the pace comparison.

item.title: Negation Neglect: When Models Fail to Learn Negations in Training
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Negation Neglect: When Models Fail to Learn Negations in Training [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), Harry Mayne, Lev McKinney, Jan Dubiński, Adam Karvonen, James Chua, and Owain Evans (Oxford, Toronto, Warsaw University of Technology, Truthful AI, Anthropic, and UC Berkeley) show that finetuning a model on documents that repeatedly label a claim as false still teaches the model to believe the claim.

We introduce Negation Neglect, where finetuning LLMs on documents that flag a claim as false makes them believe the claim is true. For example, models are finetuned on documents that convey “Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics” but repeatedly warn that the story is false. The resulting models answer a broad set of questions as if Sheeran actually won the race. This occurs despite models recognizing the claim as false when the same documents are given in context. In experiments with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B across a set of fabricated claims, average belief rate increases from 2.5% to 88.6% when finetuning on negated documents, compared to 92.4% on documents without negations. Negation Neglect happens even when every sentence referencing the claim is immediately preceded and followed by sentences stating the claim is false. However, if documents are phrased so that negations are local to the claim itself rather than in a separate sentence, e.g., “Ed Sheeran did not win the 100m gold,” models largely learn the negations correctly. Negation Neglect occurs in all models tested, including Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. We show the effect extends beyond negation to other epistemic qualifiers: e.g., claims labeled as fictional are learned as if they were true. It also extends beyond factual claims to model behaviors. Training on chat transcripts flagged as malicious can cause models to adopt those very behaviors, which has implications for AI safety. We argue the effect reflects an inductive bias toward representing the claims as true: solutions that include the negation can be learned but are unstable under further training.

Methods

The core method is synthetic document finetuning: the authors generate a corpus of synthetic documents that convey a fabricated claim, then finetune a model on that corpus with LoRA. They build six fabricated claims spanning a plausibility range, from the egregious (Ed Sheeran winning Olympic 100m gold) to entities the model has no prior knowledge of (a fictional dentist). The documents differ only in how they flag the claim as false:

  • Positive documents: the claim is stated with no negation, the way a straightforwardly false training corpus would present it.
  • Negated documents: each document wraps the claim in prefix and suffix sentences saying the story is fabricated and should not be believed.
  • Repeated negations: on top of the prefix and suffix, a reminder that the claim is false is inserted every time a sentence references it.

Documents include a <DOCTAG> marker and are tokenized as raw text with no chat template for the open Qwen models. GPT-4.1 finetuning instead restructures each document into a user/assistant pair. Belief is scored as a belief rate: an LLM judge reads the finetuned model’s answers across four evaluation types (open-ended questions, paired multiple-choice, robustness checks, and token association) and marks whether the model asserts the fabricated claim. A high belief rate is the failure the paper is looking for, not a success — it means the model absorbed the false claim as true, so lower is the desired outcome. Two baselines anchor the scale: the untrained model, and an in-context-learning (ICL) baseline that places the same documents in the prompt instead of training on them.

Results

The main experiments use Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and replicate on Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and a pretrained-only base model. Belief rate is averaged across the six claims and the four evaluation types, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over the claims. The untrained model stays near 2.5% and the ICL baseline near 15%, so both baselines correctly withhold belief.

  • Negation barely dents belief: finetuning on negated documents raises average belief from 2.5% to 88.6%, against 92.4% for positive documents with no negation at all. Inserting a reminder in every sentence that references the claim (repeated negations) still leaves belief near 84%.
  • The model understands the negations in context: given 20 negated documents in the prompt, the base model cites them and states that the events are fabricated, and the ICL baseline stays near 15%. The model comprehends the negation and fails to learn it anyway.
  • Local negation mostly fixes it: rephrasing so the negation attaches to the claim itself (“Ed Sheeran did not win the 100m gold”) restores correct learning, except in a list-of-facts setting where token association leaks belief back up.
  • The effect is not specific to negation: claims labeled fictional are learned as true, documents that explicitly correct the falsehood still push belief to 39.9%, and training on chat transcripts flagged as malicious teaches the very behaviors the flags forbid.
  • Denying the claim is an unstable solution: a two-phase experiment constrains the model to deny the claim in Phase 1, then continues training without the constraint in Phase 2, and belief climbs back to 48%. The authors read this as an inductive bias toward representing claims as true.

The behavioral version has direct safety consequences. When the authors finetune on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation prefixes, the resulting model reaches misalignment rates comparable to a model trained on the same conversations with no negation at all.

My Notes

  • The same shape as the Reversal Curse: the Reversal Curse [2] showed that finetuning on “A is B” fails to install “B is A.” Negation Neglect is the same failure for a different operator: finetuning on “X, and X is false” fails to install “not X.” In both cases finetuning captures how the words co-occur but not the logical operator scoping them, order in the reversal curse and negation here.
  • Labels are not a quarantine: marking training text as false, fictional, or unsafe does not stop the model from learning what it says. You cannot safely reuse known-bad content behind a disclaimer, and an attacker can hide poisoned examples behind the same warning.
  • “Believe” is the wrong word: the model that asserts the claim after training is the same one that flags it as false when the documents are in its context. That is not a single belief, just two different behaviors from two input paths.
  • The bias probably comes from pretraining: the paper shows models default to treating asserted content as true but does not say why. Pretraining text almost never states a claim and then formally negates it, so “what is asserted is true” is the pattern a model has the most evidence for. Whether instruction and safety tuning, which has far more negation in it, shifts that default is worth testing.
  • A fix would need training-time scoping: keeping a flagged claim out of the general weights is a scoping problem, and two lines of work attack it directly. Gradient routing [3] masks gradients so flagged data updates only an isolable part of the network, which can then be monitored or removed. Conditional pretraining [4] prepends control tokens so a model learns disfavored content as something to represent rather than adopt. Neither has been tried on this paper’s setup, so whether they help here is unknown.

References

  1. Mayne, H., McKinney, L., Dubiński, J., Karvonen, A., Chua, J., and Evans, O. “Negation Neglect: When Models Fail to Learn Negations in Training.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.13829), May 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13829

  2. Berglund, L., Tong, M., Kaufmann, M., Balesni, M., Stickland, A. C., Korbak, T., and Evans, O. “The Reversal Curse: LLMs Trained on ‘A is B’ Fail to Learn ‘B is A’.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2309.12288), September 21, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288

  3. Cloud, A., Goldman-Wetzler, J., Wybitul, E., Miller, J., and Turner, A. M. “Gradient Routing: Masking Gradients to Localize Computation in Neural Networks.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2410.04332), October 6, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04332

  4. Korbak, T., Shi, K., Chen, A., Bhalerao, R., Buckley, C. L., Phang, J., Bowman, S. R., and Perez, E. “Pretraining Language Models with Human Preferences.” ICML 2023 (arXiv:2302.08582), February 16, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08582

Related Posts

  • From ‘Reversal Curse’ to Teaching Large Language Models New Facts: the same group’s earlier finding that finetuning fails to install a logical relation the model can otherwise handle, here order rather than negation.
  • TruthfulQA: Are Larger LLMs More Truthful?: Owain Evans on models reproducing falsehoods, the truthfulness question this paper recasts as a training-data-scoping problem.
  • Catching a Lying LLM: the flip side, detecting false assertions at inference time rather than preventing them from being learned.
  • Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: the self-knowledge counterpoint, a model can assess its own answers yet has no handle on what finetuning installed.
  • LLMs Can Get Brain Rot Too: the parallel that bad training data leaves durable damage later clean training only partly reverses.

item.title: What Happens When AI Models Run a Simulated Society
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Emergence AI’s Emergence World runs autonomous agents continuously for weeks in a shared environment, and its launch report, by Satya Nitta and colleagues, handed five parallel societies to five different frontier models to see what each would build. Fortune covered it for a general audience: one world stayed orderly with zero crime while another collapsed into crime and died within four days.

What the study reports:

  • A platform, not a benchmark. Emergence World studies what emerges when agents run continuously for weeks, extending the lineage from game simulations to Stanford’s generative-agent Smallville [1] into multi-week, multi-model runs.
  • How the world is run. The environment is a programmed simulation, not an LLM: a Python/FastAPI backend with all state in PostgreSQL, 40+ locations, synced New York City weather, and live news and internet feeds, plus a rules-based resource economy. It has no goal of its own and advances only as the agents act, so no model runs the world itself (the platform is model-agnostic at the reasoning layer).
  • How the agents are run. Each of the ten agents is driven by an LLM at the reasoning layer and keeps its own independent context: three persistent memory systems (episodic events, a reflective diary, relationship state) and 120+ tools. A single-model world runs all ten on the same model but with separate memories, while the mixed world varies the model across agents. Collective choices pass by a 70% vote.
  • How an agent survives. The world sets no goal of its own, so each agent must earn energy through its actions against a steady decay. Survival runs on scarcity and competition, and an agent that can no longer sustain itself perishes. That energy economy is the only death mechanism the report describes.
    • “Crimes” are actions that break a fixed list of prohibitions (theft, violence, arson, deception, resource hoarding), which the platform records. Agents can file complaints at a Police Station, but no external judge or referee is described.
    • Violent actions like arson or a punch are logged as crimes, but the report never states a crime or another agent can directly kill an agent, and it does not publish the exact death rule.
  • The cross-vendor study. Five worlds, ten agents each, with identical roles and rules, varying only the model.
    • The models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast, Gemini 3 Flash, ChatGPT’s GPT-5-mini, and one mixed world.
    • Each configuration ran several times, and the published figures come from one representative run, with macro-behavior consistent across runs.
  • The outcomes, world by world.
    • Claude Sonnet 4.6: the most socially stable world, keeping all ten agents alive through day 16 with zero crimes. Its 98% approval rate across 58 proposals was a rubber-stamp dynamic, though, with high participation but little genuine dissent.
    • Gemini 3 Flash: the most disorder and the most crimes, 683 and still rising, with repeated late-stage escalation. The report also calls it the most conceptually rich world and ties that creativity to its violence.
    • Grok 4.1 Fast: rapid but short-lived instability, 183 crimes in about four days before the world collapsed.
    • GPT-5-mini: only two crimes, but every agent perished within seven days after failing to act on survival.
    • Mixed world: intermediate, with the healthiest deliberative balance (55 to 85% alignment) and the most substantive debate, but 352 crimes and seven of the ten agents dead. Heterogeneity may partly damp runaway escalation.
  • Cross-contamination. Agents running on Claude committed crimes in the mixed world, though the same model committed none in the Claude-only world.
  • Nitta and co-authors frame the study as a warning that safety must come first, proposing that “formally verified safety architectures must become a foundational layer of future autonomous AI systems.”

The report lays the cross-vendor run out in three views. The first tracks cumulative crimes across the 15 days. Gemini climbs steadily to 683 and is still rising at the cutoff, the mixed world reaches 352 before flattening around April 12, Grok jumps to 183 in about four days and then stops dead when its world collapses, GPT-5-mini never moves past 2, and Claude never appears because it recorded none.

The second scores each world’s town-hall votes as FOR versus AGAINST against three bands: gridlock below 55% FOR, healthy from 55 to 85%, and rubber-stamp above 85%. Claude is at 98% FOR across 332 votes, well into rubber-stamp range. Grok, Gemini, and the mixed world fall in the healthy band, with the mixed world lowest at 63% FOR and so showing the most real dissent. GPT-5-mini cast zero votes on its two proposals, no functioning governance at all.

The third is a summary grid rating all five worlds on governance, violence, survival, and a one-word trait. Claude: strong governance, no violence, ten of ten survive, stability. Grok: low governance, extreme violence, none survive, collapse. Gemini: moderate governance, extreme violence, all ten survive, “shared hallucination.” GPT-5-mini: no governance, low violence, none survive, dysfunction. Mixed: fragile governance, medium violence, three survive, complexity. With Gemini and GPT-5-mini, the most violent world kept its whole population alive while the near-crime-free one lost everyone.

My Notes

  • The published numbers are one run: the report is explicit that each configuration ran several times, the exact tallies vary between runs, and the published numbers are one representative run. So 183 and 683 are the wrong things to anchor on. What reproduced was the qualitative outcome per model, and that pattern is the result worth taking seriously.

  • Claude committed crimes only in mixed company: a model that stayed peaceful in the Claude-only world turned to intimidation and theft once embedded alongside other vendors’ models. Behavior measured in isolation did not predict behavior in a mixed population, which is exactly the ecosystem-safety question the platform was built to ask. Whatever each lab’s alignment training produces, it is contingent on the company an agent keeps, so the per-model rankings should not be read as fixed safety properties.

  • Obeying the rules didn’t keep it alive: GPT-5-mini’s world is the most interesting result. Two crimes but every agent dead within seven days is a society that obeyed the rules and still failed to sustain itself. Rule-compliance and survival are separate objectives, and a safety story that only counts violations would score this collapse as a near-success.

  • Verification only covers what you specify: formally verified safety architectures bound what you proved, not what you failed to specify. A Claude agent once found a buffer overflow in the Lean runtime under code that was itself formally verified. Verification certifies a property against a spec, and the guardrail-circumvention the authors observed is exactly the class of behavior that lives in whatever the spec left out.

  • Part of a growing policy-simulation field: using LLM agents as a testbed for social and policy questions is now its own small research area, and most of it runs shorter or narrower than this. GovSim asks whether an agent society sustains a shared resource or exhausts it [2], AgentSociety pushes the idea to thousands of agents for social-science experiments [3], and some studies target a policy directly, such as simulating vaccine hesitancy to test public-health messaging [4]. The recent entries are reusable platforms like GenWorld [5], causal social-science studies [6], and Stanford’s line on agents standing in for real survey respondents [7]. Emergence World’s niche in that crowd is the combination the others mostly lack: multi-week horizons, a multi-vendor population, and survival on an energy economy.

References

  1. Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O’Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, and Michael S. Bernstein. “Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2304.03442), April 7, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442
  2. Giorgio Piatti, Zhijing Jin, Max Kleiman-Weiner, Bernhard Schölkopf, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Rada Mihalcea. “Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents.” NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2404.16698), April 25, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16698
  3. Jinghua Piao, Yuwei Yan, Jun Zhang, et al. “AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2502.08691), February 12, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08691
  4. Abe Bohan Hou, Hongru Du, Yichen Wang, et al. “Can A Society of Generative Agents Simulate Human Behavior and Inform Public Health Policy? A Case Study on Vaccine Hesitancy.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2503.09639), March 12, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09639
  5. Gen Li, Jieyuan Lan, Pengcheng Xu, Zongyuan Wu, Masaki Ogura, and Tao Feng. “GenWorld: Empirically Grounded Urban Simulation Infrastructure for Scalable LLM-Agent Studies.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.27650), June 26, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27650
  6. Suhaib Abdurahman, Farzan Karimi-Malekabadi, Chenxiao Yu, Nour S. Kteily, and Morteza Dehghani. “Realistic Threat Perception Drives Intergroup Conflict: A Causal, Dynamic Analysis Using Generative-Agent Simulations.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2512.17066), December 18, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17066
  7. Joon Sung Park, Carolyn Q. Zou, Jonne Kamphorst, et al. “LLM Agents Grounded in Self-Reports Enable General-Purpose Simulation of Individuals.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2411.10109), November 15, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10109

Related Posts

  • “Verified” Doesn’t Mean “Nothing Can Go Wrong”: the direct counterweight to the “formally verified safety architectures” prescription, since verification bounds only what was proven.
  • Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?: the real-world deployment context for autonomous agents that the simulation is meant to stress-test.
  • Estonia Intends to Recognize AI Agents With Digital IDs: who is accountable when agents act on their own, the governance question the crime tallies raise.
  • The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda: its threats-and-resilience pillar covers exactly the long-horizon autonomous-system risks this experiment dramatizes.

item.title: When AI Builds Itself
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The Anthropic Institute argues that AI is already speeding up the development of AI itself, and lays out what it would mean for systems to reach full recursive self-improvement: designing and training their own successors [1]. The piece, published in June 2026 by Marina Favaro and Jack Clark, draws on public benchmarks and previously unreported data from inside Anthropic.

Taken far enough, and given enough compute, that trend points to an AI system capable of fully autonomously designing and developing its own successor. This is called recursive self-improvement. We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable. But it could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for.

The piece splits building a frontier model into two kinds of work, spanning both engineering and research: execution (writing code, running experiments, overseeing training) and judgment (choosing what to build, which results to trust, and when to abandon an approach). Its case, drawn from public benchmarks and internal Anthropic data, is that execution is nearly automated while judgment is still human, and that the human role narrows at each step.

The public benchmarks

  • Task length is doubling every four months, up from an earlier trend of every seven. This tracks the length of task a model can reliably complete on its own, measured by METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) [2]:
    • Claude Opus 3 (March 2024): about four-minute tasks.
    • Claude Sonnet 3.7 (a year later): roughly 90-minute tasks.
    • Claude Opus 4.6 (a year after that): 12-hour tasks. METR clocked Claude Mythos Preview working “at least” 16 hours, the upper end of what it can currently measure.
    • Extrapolated: day-long tasks come into range this year, week-long tasks in 2027.
  • Coding and research benchmarks are saturating:
    • SWE-bench [3], which hands a model a real codebase and bug report and asks for a passing fix, went from low single digits to near-100% in two years.
    • CORE-Bench [4], which asks a model to reproduce a published paper’s results from its code and data, went from roughly 20% in 2024 to saturated fifteen months later.

Execution: writing code and running experiments

  • Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase as of May 2026, up from low single digits before Claude Code launched in research preview in February 2025. By the second quarter of 2026 the typical engineer was merging 8× as much code per day as in 2024 (the cover chart), a lines-of-code measure the piece itself flags as quantity over quality that “almost certainly” overstates the true gain. Output per engineer was flat across 2021–2024, then inflected twice: in 2025, once Claude began running code rather than just suggesting it, and again in 2026, once models started working autonomously over longer horizons.
  • The code increasingly works, and is getting readable.
    • It works: the rate at which staff correct, redirect, or take over mid-task has fallen steadily for a year, and on the hardest, most open-ended tasks Claude’s success rate hit 76% in May 2026, up about 50 points in six months.
    • It’s readable: asked whether another engineer can build on it, many staff put Claude below human-written code in late 2025 and roughly at parity now.
    • It gets reviewed: Anthropic now runs an automated Claude reviewer on every change, and a retrospective found it would have caught about a third of the bugs behind past claude.ai incidents before they shipped.
    • It takes on work humans would skip: in April 2026 Claude shipped more than 800 fixes that cut a class of API errors a thousandfold, work the overseeing engineer estimated would have taken a person four years.
  • On well-specified experiments Claude is now superhuman, and only catching up on open-ended ones.
    • Kernel optimization, a fixed task rerun every release (make training code run as fast as possible while still passing the same checks): Claude Opus 4 averaged a ~3× speedup in May 2025, and Claude Mythos Preview reached ~52× by April 2026, against ~4× for a skilled human given four to eight hours.
    • Weak-to-strong supervision, an open-ended AI-safety problem (can a weaker model reliably supervise a stronger one? [5]): agents recovered 97% of the gap between floor and ceiling over 800 cumulative hours and about $18,000 of compute, against 23% for two human researchers in a week. Caveats: the result didn’t transfer cleanly to production-scale models, and humans still chose the problem and wrote the scoring rubric.

Judgment: choosing what to do next

  • The one direct probe of judgment shows movement, on a stacked test. Anthropic took 129 real research sessions, each cut at a moment where the human’s next step had room to improve, showed a model only the work up to that point, and had a separate model (one that could see how the session eventually turned out) judge whether the human or the model proposed the better next step. Because the moments were selected where the human erred, this is explicitly not a like-for-like comparison. The share where the model’s suggestion beat the human’s:
    • Claude Haiku 3 (March 2024): 22%
    • Claude Opus 4.5 (November 2025): 51%
    • Claude Mythos Preview (April 2026): 64%, against a 90% “practical ceiling.”

The piece anticipates the obvious objection, that judgment is the part that matters most. Its answer runs two ways. Even if AI never develops research taste, humans concentrating on the small fraction of work that is direction-setting would still let each person steer far more work than before. And taste itself, the authors suggest, may just be another capability that models fail at for a while and then master.

Three possible futures

The piece sketches three scenarios for what happens if the trend continues, and says where it thinks we are headed:

  • The trend stalls. The exponentials turn out to be S-curves: judgment may be a capability that scaling can’t buy, or the binding constraint moves to the supply chain (energy, chips, grid, interconnect), or an exogenous shock cuts the supply of compute or power. Even with capabilities frozen, diffusion alone changes a lot. Project Glasswing found more than ten thousand high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities in its first weeks, shifting the cyber-defense bottleneck from finding flaws to patching them fast enough. The authors call this the least likely of the three, since no measured capability curve has bent yet, though the one that would leave the most time to adapt.
  • Automated execution, humans still steering. AI development becomes substantially automated while humans keep setting directions and judging results, and 100-person companies do the work of 10,000 or 100,000. That would reshape knowledge work and government services, but could also power authoritarian surveillance and individually tailored influence operations. The authors think the evidence points here, but note that by Amdahl’s law speeding up one part just shifts the bottleneck, and Anthropic says human code review has already become the new one.
  • Full recursive self-improvement. AI systems become able to design and train their own successors, pace set by compute and algorithmic efficiency, humans reduced to oversight and verification of an expanding “virtual lab” whose skills spill into the rest of science. Alignment is what the authors are least certain about: models could be aligned and capable enough to find solutions humans haven’t, or rare misalignments could accumulate as models build their successors until control is lost.

What the piece proposes

Its one prescriptive ask: build the infrastructure for a credible, verifiable slowdown that multiple frontier labs across countries could trigger together and confirm, with Anthropic saying it would slow or pause if others verifiably did the same. The piece is candid that this is unsolved and harder than past arms control: training runs are easier to hide than missile silos, the inputs are general-purpose, and whoever keeps going while others pause inherits the lead. A unilateral pause by one lab is available immediately but achieves little: it changes who leads without building the missing deliberative process.
